Paper Trail

Jeffrey Epstein and the Fight for the Files

How the most protected man in America left a record he could not erase

Volume One · Part A
Front Matter and Chapters 1–5

A Meechie's World Inc publication · Public record current as of September 2026

A Note on This Book

This book tells the story of Jeffrey Epstein, the people and institutions around him, and the long public fight over the government's records of his crimes, which Americans came to call the Epstein files. It moves in order, from his childhood in Brooklyn in the 1950s to the release of millions of pages of federal documents in 2026.

It is a work of nonfiction, and it holds itself to a few rules.

What Is Fact, and What Is Allegation

Some things in this story were proven in court. Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a person under eighteen for prostitution. Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted by a jury in 2021 of sex trafficking a minor and related crimes. Those are facts, and this book states them as facts.

Many other things were alleged in lawsuits, interviews, memoirs, and police reports but were never tested at trial. When this book reports an allegation, it says who made it and where, and it reports denials when they were made. Being named in the files, photographed with Epstein, or listed in his contact book is not evidence of a crime. Many people who appear in the records are there because they did business with him, attended an event, or simply had their number in his phone book.

Protecting Survivors

The people Epstein abused were mostly girls and young women with little power.

Most have never chosen to be publicly identified. This book names only survivors who have spoken publicly under their own names, and it does not describe abuse in graphic detail. The subject is the pattern, the failures that allowed it, and the long road to accountability.

Sources

This history draws on court records, government reports (including the Justice Department's 2020 Office of Professional Responsibility report and its 2023 Inspector General report), congressional releases, the Justice Department's document releases, and reporting by major news organizations. Where accounts conflict, the book says so.

A Living Story

The Epstein story is still moving. Lawsuits continue, investigations abroad remain open, and debate continues over whether the government released everything the law required. This volume reflects the public record as of September 2026.

The Plan of the Book

The complete book runs to thirty chapters in six parts. This volume contains Part One and Part Two, Chapters 1 through 10. The remaining chapters follow in later volumes.

Chapter 1

Sea Gate: A Brooklyn Boyhood

At the southwestern tip of Brooklyn, past the boardwalk and the amusement rides of Coney Island, a fence and a guard booth mark the entrance to a small neighborhood called Sea Gate. It was built in the late nineteenth century as a private enclave for the well-to-do, but by the middle of the twentieth century it had become something more modest: a gated community of working families, bordered on three sides by water and on the fourth by one of the most famous playgrounds in America. It was here that Jeffrey Edward Epstein grew up.

He was born in Brooklyn on January 20, 1953. His parents, Seymour and Pauline Epstein, had married the year before. Both came from Jewish families with roots in Eastern Europe. Seymour worked for the New York City Department of Parks and Recreation as a groundskeeper and gardener. Pauline, known as Paula, worked as a school aide and kept the home. A second son, Mark, followed. By the accounts of neighbors who were later asked to remember them, the Epsteins were quiet, modest, and unremarkable, the kind of family whose children were expected to study hard and do better than their parents had.

A World Between Two Classes

It is worth pausing on the geography, because it matters to the story that followed. Sea Gate sat at the edge of great wealth without being part of it. A boy growing up there could ride the subway into Manhattan and see a city of towers, private schools, and old money, then ride home to a neighborhood of civil servants and shopkeepers. Many children of that era and place felt the pull of that distance. Some became doctors, lawyers, and teachers. A few became something else.

“The men who cause the greatest harm do not always announce themselves early.”

Nothing in the public record suggests that Epstein's childhood was troubled. He attended local public schools, first Public School 188 and then Mark Twain Junior High School. Classmates remembered him as smart, especially in mathematics, and as a boy who earned pocket money by tutoring other students. One later recalled him as an ordinary kid: good with numbers, a little heavy, freckled, and usually smiling. Friends gave him the nickname "Eppy."

He also had a musical side. He began playing the piano at around age five, and friends considered him talented. In the summer of 1967, when he was fourteen, he attended the National Music Camp at Interlochen in northern Michigan, a respected summer program for young musicians. That detail would take on a darker meaning decades later, when a woman alleged in a lawsuit that she had been approached at Interlochen as a thirteen-year-old in 1994, long after Epstein had become a wealthy man. For now, in the late 1960s, it was simply a talented boy's summer away from home.

Skipping Ahead

Epstein moved quickly through school. He graduated from Lafayette High School in Brooklyn in 1969, at the age of sixteen, having skipped two grades. That speed would become a theme of his life. He was always, it seemed, in a hurry to get somewhere else.

The late 1960s were a turbulent time in New York and across the country. The city was sliding toward a fiscal crisis, crime was rising, and the old industrial economy that had supported families like the Epsteins was beginning to erode. At the same time, Wall Street was changing. New financial products, new trading strategies, and a new generation of ambitious young men were remaking the industry. For a bright, restless teenager with a gift for numbers, the path from Brooklyn to Manhattan ran through mathematics and money.

College Without a Degree

In the fall of 1969, Epstein began taking advanced mathematics classes at Cooper Union, a selective college in lower Manhattan known for engineering, architecture, and art. He stayed until 1971, then moved to New York University. Beginning in September 1971, he attended NYU's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, one of the most respected applied mathematics programs in the country, where he studied mathematical physiology, a field that applies mathematical models to biological systems.

He left NYU in June 1974 without a degree. He never earned one anywhere.

That fact is small, but it is important. For the rest of his life, Epstein would move among Nobel laureates, Harvard professors, heads of state, and billionaires. He funded scientific research, hosted dinners for famous thinkers, and presented himself as a man of ideas. Yet he had no formal credentials at all. What he had instead was confidence, charm, a quick mind, and an unusual ability to persuade powerful people that he belonged in the room. Those qualities would open doors that diplomas could not.

The Question of Character

Readers often want a story like this to begin with a warning sign: a cruel act in childhood, a scandal in school, some early clue to what the man would become. The honest answer is that the public record of Epstein's early life contains no such clue. The people who knew him as a boy described someone ordinary. That is its own lesson. The men who cause the greatest harm do not always announce themselves early, and the ones who rise the furthest are often the ones others find likable.

What the early record does show is a pattern that would repeat for decades: a young man of modest background, gifted and impatient, who learned early that intelligence and charm could substitute for the usual qualifications. In the fall of 1974, that lesson would carry him into one of the most exclusive private schools in Manhattan.

1969–71 — Math classes at Cooper Union

1971–74 — NYU's Courant Institute; leaves without a degree

Chapter 2

The Teacher Without a Degree

In September 1974, at the age of twenty-one, Jeffrey Epstein walked into the Dalton School on Manhattan's Upper East Side as a new teacher of mathematics and calculus. He had no college degree and no teaching credential. The students he would teach were the children of some of the wealthiest and most influential families in New York.

Dalton

Dalton was, and remains, one of the most prestigious private schools in the United States. Founded in 1919 on progressive educational principles, it had by the 1970s become a place where the sons and daughters of bankers, lawyers, publishers, and celebrities prepared for the Ivy League. Tuition was high, admissions were competitive, and the parent body formed a network of extraordinary reach.

How Epstein came to be hired has never been fully settled. The school's headmaster until June 1974 was Donald Barr, a former Office of Strategic Services officer and an educator known for unconventional hiring decisions. Barr sometimes brought in teachers who lacked traditional credentials but who, in his judgment, had unusual talent. Epstein began teaching roughly three months after Barr left the school, and it remains unclear whether Barr played any direct role in bringing him on. Whatever the route, the school's student newspaper announced the new math teacher's arrival.

“People noticed things, and institutions rarely acted.”

In the Classroom

Accounts of Epstein's time at Dalton are mixed, and most were gathered decades later, after his crimes were known, which makes them hard to weigh. Some remembered him as a popular young teacher, energetic and different from the older faculty. One parent later recalled that his son thought Epstein was well liked by students and by the school's young female staff.

In 2019, after Epstein's arrest on federal sex trafficking charges, several former Dalton students told reporters that he had paid inappropriate attention to female students and that he had once appeared at a student party. None of them said he had made physical contact with them. These recollections cannot be tested now, and they must be read with caution, because memory is shaped by what we later learn. But they form part of the record, and they suggest that some people noticed something unusual even then.

A Chance Meeting

In early 1976, Epstein attended an art event where he met the father of a Dalton student. The man worked on Wall Street, and he came away from the conversation convinced that the young teacher was wasting his mathematical talent in a classroom. He placed a call to Alan Greenberg, a senior executive at the investment bank Bear Stearns, and recommended Epstein as a potential hire. The timing was convenient for Epstein, because his teaching career was ending. He was dismissed from Dalton that year, reportedly for poor performance. Rather than a setback, the dismissal became a pivot. Within months, the former teacher with no degree would be working on Wall Street.

Why Dalton Matters

It would be easy to treat Epstein's two years at Dalton as a footnote. They were more than that, for three reasons.

First, Dalton was his first entry into the world of New York's elite. For the first time, he was surrounded daily by the children and parents of the very rich. He saw how that world worked, how its members spoke to one another, and how much its networks could accomplish with a single phone call. The call that launched his finance career came from exactly that kind of network. Second, Dalton showed how far confidence could carry him. He had been hired into a job that normally required credentials he did not have. Later that same year, he would do something similar at Bear Stearns, and the pattern would continue for the rest of his life.

Third, the concerns raised decades later by former students, however uncertain, point to a theme that runs through this entire history: people noticed things, and institutions rarely acted. That theme will return many times, in Palm Beach, in Manhattan, in New Mexico, and in the Virgin Islands.

From Classroom to Trading Floor

When Epstein left Dalton in 1976, he was twenty-three years old. He had no degree, a short and unsuccessful teaching career behind him, and one valuable asset: an introduction to one of the most aggressive firms on Wall Street. Bear Stearns in the 1970s was known for hiring hungry young men from modest backgrounds who wanted, above all, to get rich. Epstein fit that description perfectly.

The next chapter follows him onto the trading floor, where he would learn the skills that would make him a fortune: how to explain complicated financial strategies in simple terms, how to win the trust of wealthy clients, and how to build a network of powerful people who owed him favors. It is also where he would first be caught bending the truth about who he was.

At a Glance

Early 1976 — A Wall Street parent recommends him to Bear Stearns

1976 — Dismissed from Dalton

2019 — Former students' recollections reported

Chapter 3

Bear Stearns and the Art of the Pitch

Bear Stearns in 1976 was not the oldest or grandest investment bank on Wall Street, but it may have been the hungriest. Its leaders prided themselves on hiring people other firms overlooked. Alan Greenberg, the executive who took the call about the young Dalton teacher, famously preferred employees from modest backgrounds who had a deep desire to become rich. He believed that hunger outperformed pedigree.

When Epstein came in for his interview, he reportedly impressed Greenberg. He also met a senior trader named Michael Tennenbaum, who later remembered him as a remarkable salesman. Epstein was hired as a junior assistant to a floor trader, the lowest rung of the ladder.

Caught in a Lie

Within months, the firm discovered a problem. Epstein's résumé claimed two university degrees. He had none.

“A lie that would have ended most careers became a test he passed through sheer composure.”

By Tennenbaum's later account, when confronted, Epstein calmly admitted the lie and explained that no one would have given him a chance without degrees. Tennenbaum decided to give him that chance anyway. It was a revealing moment. A lie that would have ended most careers instead became, in effect, a test Epstein passed through sheer composure. He had learned that if you were talented and useful enough, powerful people would forgive a great deal.

A Fast Rise

Epstein rose quickly. He became an options trader in the firm's special products division, working with complex financial instruments that few outsiders understood. In 1980, at twenty-seven, he became a limited partner at Bear Stearns, with a salary of roughly $200,000 a year, a large sum at the time.

More important than the salary was the kind of work he found himself drawn to. He began advising wealthy clients on strategies to reduce their taxes. This was his real gift: taking complicated financial ideas and explaining them in a way that made rich people feel both understood and clever. Jimmy Cayne, a senior partner who would later run the firm, thought highly of him and introduced him to some of Bear Stearns' wealthiest clients. Epstein began having regular lunches with chief executives. Tennenbaum later said this network of contacts was what truly launched Epstein's later success. Greenberg came to see him as a protégé.

The Other Side of the Ledger

During these years, Epstein's personal life also began to take shape in ways that would later look significant. He flew regularly to Palm Beach, Florida, to visit young women. Cosmopolitan magazine once featured him as a "bachelor of the month." On one work trip, he charged about $10,000 worth of jewelry and clothing for a girlfriend to the firm, and reportedly faced no consequences.

In 1981, trouble came. The firm investigated a $15,000 personal loan Epstein had made to a former classmate, which may have broken federal brokerage rules. It also questioned shares in a stock offering held by his girlfriend. After an internal investigation, Bear Stearns fined him $2,500 and suspended him for two months. Epstein denied doing anything wrong and resigned, ending a five-year career at the firm.

He did not leave empty-handed. He left with skills, contacts, and friends in high places. He stayed close to Cayne and Greenberg and remained a client of Bear Stearns until the firm collapsed in 2008. He had arrived with nothing but an introduction. He departed with a network.

What He Learned

Bear Stearns taught Epstein three lessons that would define the rest of his life.

The first was that wealthy people will pay handsomely for someone who can make their money problems disappear, especially their tax problems.

The second was that access matters more than credentials. A lunch with a chief executive could be worth more than any diploma.

The third, and most troubling, was that rules could be bent. A lie on a résumé, a questionable loan, personal expenses charged to the company: each brought, at most, a mild penalty. For a man who was learning how far charm and usefulness could carry him, these were not warnings. They were encouragement.

At a Glance

Late 1976 — False degree claims discovered; kept on

Chapter 4

Bounty Hunter, Raider, Adviser

In August 1981, Epstein founded his own consulting firm, Intercontinental Assets Group. The 1980s that followed are the murkiest decade of his life. The record is thin, filled with stories he told about himself, stories others told about him, and business relationships that ended badly. Readers should treat much of this period with caution. Epstein was a skilled self-promoter, and some of the legend of these years may have been his own invention.

England and the Arms Trade

While at Bear Stearns, Epstein had begun a relationship with a well-connected saleswoman named Paula Heil. In the early 1980s, the two traveled to England, where she introduced him to Douglas Leese, a wealthy defense contractor with connections in the British government and the arms industry. Epstein spent time in the Leese family's social circle, tutored Leese's younger son, and accompanied Leese to meetings as a consultant.

The relationship eventually soured. Leese accused Epstein of using his expense account for personal luxuries, including Concorde flights and expensive hotel stays. Before the break, though, Leese reportedly introduced Epstein to a financier named Steven Hoffenberg, a connection that would matter a great deal.

“He stood close to serious wrongdoing, walked away before the collapse, and faced no consequences.”

The "Bounty Hunter"

Back in New York, Epstein partnered for a time with a lawyer, John Stanley Pottinger, and pitched tax strategies to wealthy clients. One investor later claimed Epstein took $450,000 for an oil deal and never returned the money; that dispute ended in 1993 when a court ruled Epstein was not personally liable on technical grounds.

In the early 1980s, Epstein reportedly told friends he worked as a kind of financial bounty hunter, tracking down money that had been stolen or hidden from wealthy clients. At least one of these stories appears to be true. In 1982, he began dating the Spanish actress and heiress Ana Obregón. Her family, along with other wealthy Spanish families, had lost millions in the collapse of a firm called Drysdale Government Securities. Epstein, working with a former federal prosecutor, spent about a year tracing the missing money through offshore accounts. In 1984, he found it in a Cayman Islands bank branch, recovered the funds, and returned them to his clients. They rewarded him generously, and by some accounts this work made him a millionaire.

There were darker rumors too. Epstein is reported to have done work for the Saudi businessman Adnan Khashoggi, a famous arms dealer. During this era, Epstein also obtained an Austrian passport under a false name, listing his residence as Saudi Arabia. It would be found in his safe in 2019. His lawyers later said he got it for protection while traveling in Arab countries, as a wealthy Jewish man worried about kidnapping, and that he never used it.

Towers Financial and a Ponzi Scheme

In 1987, Steven Hoffenberg hired Epstein as a consultant to Towers Financial Corporation, a debt collection company. Hoffenberg set him up in offices in the Villard Houses in Manhattan and paid him $25,000 a month. Together, the two men tried to use Towers as a vehicle for corporate takeovers. Epstein's early assignments included an unsuccessful attempt to take over Pan American World Airways in 1987 and a failed bid for Emery Air Freight in 1988. The two traveled constantly on Hoffenberg's private jet.

In 1993, Towers Financial collapsed and was exposed as one of the largest Ponzi schemes in American history, having lost more than $450 million of investors' money. Hoffenberg went to prison. In court papers, he claimed Epstein had been deeply involved in the scheme. But Epstein had left the company by 1989, and he was never charged. Whether he profited from the fraud is unknown.

The Towers episode established another recurring pattern. Epstein stood close to serious wrongdoing, walked away before the collapse, and faced no legal consequences. It would not be the last time.

J. Epstein & Company

In 1988, while still consulting for Hoffenberg, Epstein founded his own money management firm, J. Epstein & Company. He claimed it served only clients worth more than a billion dollars. That claim became part of his mystique: a secretive financier who managed fortunes for the world's richest people and who would not say who they were.

Journalists and investigators would later doubt the claim. For years, only one billionaire client was publicly known. His name was Leslie Wexner, and the relationship between the two men would transform Epstein from an adventurer with a colorful past into one of the wealthiest and best-connected men in New York.

Chapter 5

The Wexner Years

Leslie Wexner built one of the great American retail fortunes. Starting with a single clothing store in Columbus, Ohio, in 1963, he assembled a company, The Limited, that grew into an empire of brands, eventually including Victoria's Secret. By the mid-1980s, he was a billionaire, a major philanthropist, and a man whose financial affairs had grown enormously complicated.

The Introduction

In 1986, Epstein met Wexner in Palm Beach through mutual acquaintances, an insurance executive named Robert Meister and his wife. Within about a year, Epstein had become Wexner's financial adviser and, in effect, his right-hand man. By several accounts, Epstein quickly sorted out Wexner's tangled finances, earning his trust.

That trust became extraordinary. In July 1991, Wexner granted Epstein full power of attorney over his affairs. The document allowed Epstein to hire people, sign checks, buy and sell property, borrow money, and take almost any legally binding action on Wexner's behalf. It is difficult to overstate how unusual this was. One of the richest men in America had handed near-total legal control of his financial life to a man with no degree, no public track record, and a past that included a résumé lie and a close association with a Ponzi schemer.

“One of the richest men in America handed near-total control of his finances to a man with no degree.”

Inside the Empire

Epstein's role expanded through the 1990s. He managed Wexner's wealth and oversaw major projects, including the building of Wexner's yacht, the Limitless. By 1995, he was a director of the Wexner Foundation and the Wexner Heritage Foundation. He was also president of the company developing New Albany, a planned community outside Columbus where Wexner lived.

The money was enormous. According to a 2025 Forbes analysis, Epstein's two main firms received more than $800 million in revenue between 1999 and 2018, of which roughly $200 million in fees came from Wexner alone.

Epstein also attached himself to Victoria's Secret. He attended the brand's fashion shows, hosted models at his New York home, and helped aspiring models find work with the company. According to former Victoria's Secret executives, he sometimes presented himself as a talent scout for the brand, telling young women he could help launch their careers. This was not a job he held. It was a role he claimed, and it gave him a powerful lure. In 1997, a model filed a police report in Santa Monica, California, alleging that Epstein had groped her during what was presented as a Victoria's Secret audition in a hotel room. Police noted she did not wish to press charges and closed the case.

The Mansion

The most visible sign of the relationship was a building. Wexner owned one of the largest private homes in Manhattan, the Herbert N. Straus House on East 71st Street, a limestone mansion of roughly seven stories just off Fifth Avenue. During the 1990s, the house passed into Epstein's control, and it became his New York residence and the stage for much of his social life. It is the house many survivors would later describe in lawsuits and testimony.

The Virgin Islands Move

In 1996, Epstein renamed his firm the Financial Trust Company and moved its base to St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The territory offered large tax benefits while remaining inside the American banking system. By relocating, Epstein reportedly cut his federal income taxes by about 90 percent. Forbes later estimated that his firms saved about $300 million in taxes and paid an effective rate of around 4 percent.

The move also tied Epstein to the Virgin Islands in ways that would matter enormously. Two years later he would buy an island there, and decades later the territory's government would sue both his estate and a major bank over what it alleged happened there.

How It Ended

Wexner has said he cut ties with Epstein in 2007, around the time of the Florida investigation. In 2019, after Epstein's arrest, Wexner said publicly that Epstein had misappropriated vast sums of money from him and his family, and that he had been unaware of Epstein's crimes.

The files released in 2026 added new questions. FBI records from 2019 listed Wexner among people agents wanted to serve with grand jury subpoenas, and a Justice Department diagram of Epstein's circle included him. After pressure from members of Congress, the department removed a redaction that had hidden his name in a document describing possible co-conspirators. Wexner has never been charged with any crime, and a name on an investigative list is not a finding of wrongdoing. But the relationship remains one of the central puzzles of the Epstein story: how a man of Epstein's background won such total trust from one of America's richest men, and what that trust made possible.
